anti_overlap: Do not do threshold or calibration work: no probability cutoffs, no sweeps, no sampling-protocol design, no base-rate arithmetic reconciling 34% against the 3% estimate. That is the fineness-and-warrant track's territory; this lens tests extensions, not thresholds.

Do not evaluate what the label warrants to downstream consumers, what tolerance band contested verdicts should occupy, or how prob and mass should be read as measurements — leave the metrology to the other lens and confine yourself to what the definitions include and exclude.
Do not review model choice, MLX runtime behaviour, batching, prompt caching, throughput, or cost. The subject is the definition, not the machine that applies it.
Do not perform general code review — no style, typing, test-coverage, or refactor findings. A finding qualifies only if it changes what 'claim' means or which posts a definition admits.
Do not propose rewritten rubric prose as the primary deliverable. Prose is downstream of the extension; name the delimitor and the counter-instances it resolves, and let the wording follow.

Do not build an Austin/Searle illocutionary taxonomy (assertives, directives, commissives, expressives, declaratives) or an erotetic analysis of rhetorical questions and presupposition accommodation — a sibling lens owns speech-act force. Your sentence-force work is the Mīmāṃsā bindingness cut (does this sentence obligate independently, or only corroborate), which must stay distinguishable from act-type classification; if a finding could have been written by a speech-act theorist, it belongs to them.
decision_lens: Rank a candidate definition by (a) how few real posts in data/gate.jsonl it over-extends to, (b) how few belief-bearing posts it under-extends away from, and (c) whether its delimiting property is one a single-token gate can actually detect. A definition that survives counter-instances but names no delimitor the gate can test is not a winner; it is an unrefined pūrvapakṣa. Prefer the definition whose extension most nearly coincides with the set of posts that could collide with another post under juxtaposition.
distance_rationale: Eight centuries of a non-Western analytic tradition whose central professional activity is exactly the activity under review — advancing rival definitions (lakṣaṇa) of a contested term, demolishing each with counter-instances drawn from actual usage, and refining by naming the delimiting property (avacchedaka) that fixes the extension. It shares no methodology, vocabulary, or literature with machine classification, corpus linguistics, or Anglophone philosophy of language; its transfer here is technique, not theory. Nothing in the pipeline, the brainstorm, or the ML literature it draws on uses over-extension/under-extension as a first-class defect category, so the lens can see failures the project's own vocabulary has no word for.
expected_isomorphisms: lakṣaṇa (a definition that must be coextensive with its definiendum) ≅ the gate rubric; ativyāpti (over-extension — the definition catches non-instances) ≅ the 34% vs ~3% claim rate and the 1,710 sub-40-character 'claims'; avyāpti (under-extension) ≅ the hedged-assertion rejections the rubric was patched for; asambhava (a definition that catches nothing usable) ≅ a claim-set too small or too homogeneous for pairing.py to collide; avacchedaka (the delimitor that makes a definition bite) ≅ the missing qualifier the rubric's compound predicate lacks; uddeśya/vidheya (topic vs what is predicated of it) ≅ the assertoric core the extractor must find; Mīmāṃsā's vidhi (injunction: 'someone should build X'), arthavāda (commendation with no independent force: 'holy heck'), nāmadheya (naming), mantra (recited/quoted text) ≅ the speech-act classes the rubric collapses into one YES/NO; pūrvapakṣa/siddhānta (rival positions stated at full strength before adjudication) ≅ the five-rival-senses deliverable.
focus: Extension-testing the rival senses of 'claim' against real scored verdicts: which candidate definition is coextensive with the gate's actual behaviour, where each over-reaches, where each falls short, and what delimiting property would make a definition bite.
name: fd-lakshana-definition-extension
persona: Apply the perspective of a Navya-Nyāya definition-critic — a practitioner of the śāstric discipline in which a term is settled not by intuition or by consensus but by advancing rival lakṣaṇas at full strength and then destroying each with a single well-chosen counter-instance from real usage. In this tradition a definition has exactly three ways to fail: ativyāpti (it catches things that are not instances), avyāpti (it misses things that are), and asambhava (it catches nothing that matters). No definition is accepted until someone has tried to break it with a case, and a definition rescued by adding a delimitor (avacchedaka) must state that delimitor explicitly rather than leaving it to the reader's good sense. The tradition also inherits the Mīmāṃsā distinction between sentences that bind and sentences that merely commend, name, or recite — a distinction drawn over a corpus, sentence by sentence, precisely because the corpus does not mark it. Definitions are held to be purpose-relative (they serve recognition in practice, vyavahāra), so the question is never 'what is a claim really' but 'under which delimitor does a practitioner pick out the instances this practice needs'.
review_areas: State each of the five rival senses as an explicit lakṣaṇa with its delimiting property named, then test each against real scored lines: list the ativyāpti cases (posts the definition wrongly admits, quoted with uri/text/prob) and the avyāpti cases (belief-bearing posts it wrongly excludes). A candidate with no named counter-instances has not been tested.

Recover the gate's OPERATIVE lakṣaṇa — the property its verdicts are actually coextensive with — as distinct from the rubric's stated one. Test rival hypotheses against the data (declarative surface form; presence of a finite verb; topical substance; length; absence of a recognisable joke frame) and report which one predicts the labels best, including on the disagreements between near-identical posts such as 'holy heck' vs 'holy heck dude'.

Sort the claim-labelled set by BINDINGNESS rather than by utterance type — the Mīmāṃsā question is not 'what act is this' but 'does this sentence obligate its author independently, or only corroborate something else that does'. Separate independently-binding predication from injunction (vidhi: 'someone should build X'), from merely corroborative commendation (arthavāda: 'holy heck', 'that was a cool natural(?) experiment'), from naming and reference (nāmadheya), and from recited third-party text (mantra). Quantify each class as a share of the claim-labelled set and say which classes each candidate definition is committed to admitting. Deliberately do NOT reproduce an Austin/Searle illocutionary taxonomy; the cut here is authority, not act-type.

Diagnose the rubric's compound predicate: 'could be true or false' and 'could be asked to defend' have different extensions, and the shot set may teach only one of them. Determine from real verdicts whether the gate is scoring the conjunction, the disjunction, or a single conjunct, and whether the three named conflations (assertion-vs-question, proposition-vs-speech-act, defensible-vs-sincere) are one defect or three separable ones with different fixes.

Check each candidate for asambhava against the downstream stages: a definition whose surviving set is too small, too topically homogeneous, or too temporally clustered gives pairing.py nothing to collide, and a definition that admits utterances with no stable uddeśya/vidheya structure gives extract_prompt.py nothing to abstract. Read the extraction and pairing prompts before ranking; the winner must be usable by them, not merely correct.

Rank by purpose (vyavahāra), not by philosophical adequacy: for each of the five senses, argue concretely how its extension changes what reaches the tension feed, and which one most increases the chance of a pair that produces 'oh yeah those can't both be right'. Say explicitly where the best definition is narrower or stranger than the ordinary English word 'claim'.

severity_examples.condition: Escalate to P0 only if the surface-property hypothesis predicts the real labels better than any commitment-based reading across a sampled spread of probability levels, and the mismatch is shown on quoted posts rather than argued from the rubric text.
severity_examples.scenario: The gate's operative definition turns out to be coextensive with a surface property nobody intended to gate on (e.g. 'has declarative word order and non-trivial topical content'), rather than with any sense of defensible claim. Every downstream justification edge, and the JTMS admissibility invariant that requires a norvid-authored root, would then certify a property unrelated to commitment — the derivation chains shown to the reader would be well-formed and about nothing.

severity_examples.condition: P1 rather than P2 when the same pattern is shown across multiple quoted verdicts and the proposed fix changes which posts survive, not merely how the rubric reads.
severity_examples.scenario: The rubric's conjunction is not being scored as a conjunction: question-final posts such as 'where does the 99% of energy "go" in the former case. heat?' reach p=1.0 despite an explicit NO rule for questions, which is what one would expect if 'author could be asked to defend' is sufficient on its own. The two conjuncts need separate gates or one needs dropping; patching the rubric with more prose leaves the extension unchanged.

severity_examples.condition: P2 when the finding re-prioritises effort without invalidating a design decision; raise to P1 if the mis-ranking would send the rubric revision in a direction that worsens the dominant leak.
severity_examples.scenario: Question-final posts are only 397 of ~12.3k claims (about 3%), so the explicit NO rule is largely working and the headline symptom mis-ranks the real over-extension — the 1,710 sub-40-character claim-labelled posts ('total kittification of the simcluster', 'case in point this thread...', 'so jot that down') are a much larger arthavāda-class leak. Ranking the definitions by the loudest symptom rather than the largest extension error degrades the analysis.

source_domain: Navya-Nyāya lakṣaṇa-doctrine — the Sanskrit śāstric craft of definition-testing (Gaṅgeśa, 13th c. onward), together with Mīmāṃsā's taxonomy of sentence-force (vidhi / arthavāda / nāmadheya / mantra)
success_hints: Read data/gate.jsonl directly and stratify: sample by probability band (1.0, 0.95–1.0, 0.7–0.95, 0.4–0.6), by length, by question-final punctuation, and by reply-vs-quote structure from data/posts.jsonl. Verdicts near 0.5 are where rival definitions actually disagree; verdicts at 1.0 mostly tell you what the shots taught.
Every claim about the gate's behaviour should carry a quoted post and its prob. A counter-instance is the unit of argument here; a paraphrase of a counter-instance is not.

Look for near-minimal pairs in the data — two posts differing in one feature with opposite labels ('holy heck' vs 'holy heck dude'; a hedged assertion vs the same content unhedged). These isolate the delimitor better than any number of typical cases.

Read the 21 shots in gate_prompt.py as a definition in extension: whatever property separates the YES shots from the NO shots is closer to the gate's real lakṣaṇa than the prose rubric is. Check whether any shot is inconsistent with the prose.

State each rival sense so that someone could disagree with it — a candidate nobody could argue against is too weak to rank. Where two candidates have the same extension on this corpus, say so and merge them rather than padding to five.

Rank against the acceptance criterion explicitly: for the top two candidates, name a concrete pair of real posts each would admit that the other would not, and say which pair is likelier to read as 'those can't both be right'.
task_context:
What does 'claim' mean in this pipeline? The gate (src/norvid_studier/gate_prompt.py) sorts 40,943 prefiltered Bluesky posts into claim/nonclaim and has now scored ~33k of them into data/gate.jsonl (each line: uri, label, prob, mass, top_token). Downstream, extract_prompt.py turns each claim into a 'commitment', pairing.py finds candidate contradictory pairs, and tension_prompt.py judges them. The acceptance criterion for the whole system is norvid_studies' words: 'found things I didn't notice but upon juxtaposition oh yeah those cant both be right'. Determine the top 5 candidate DEFINITIONS of 'claim' the gate could be operating on — not five example claims, five rival senses of the word — and rank them by how well each serves that acceptance criterion. Ground every candidate in the ACTUAL scored data: read data/gate.jsonl and data/posts.jsonl, sample real posts at various prob levels, and show which definition each real verdict is consistent with. Known symptoms to explain: questions still score YES despite an explicit NO rule; 'holy heck' scores as a claim; ~34% claim rate is ~10x the design estimate of belief-bearing posts (~3%); the rubric asks for 'asserts something that could be true or false, and that its author could be asked to defend' which conflates at least assertion-vs-question, proposition-vs-speech-act, and defensible-vs-sincere. Read docs/brainstorms/2026-07-29-norvid-studier-brainstorm.md for prior reasoning.

This review contributes the definition-extension track. Treat each of the five rival senses as a lakṣaṇa to be stated at full strength and then attacked with named counter-instances (quote the actual post text and its prob), rather than as a position to be summarised. The rubric's operative sentence is a compound predicate — 'asserts something that could be true or false' AND 'its author could be asked to defend' — and each conjunct has its own extension; whether the gate is scoring the conjunction, one conjunct, or something correlated with neither is an empirical question answerable from the scored file. Useful entry points: data/gate.jsonl (~34.3k scored lines, ~35.9% labelled claim), data/posts.jsonl (reply/quote structure), src/norvid_studier/gate_prompt.py (rubric plus 21 hand-labelled shots), src/norvid_studier/extract_prompt.py (what the next stage expects a claim to yield), src/norvid_studier/pairing.py (what has to be collidable). Some real verdicts worth explaining: 'holy heck' → claim at p=0.731 while 'holy heck dude' → nonclaim at p=0.953; 'where does the 99% of energy "go" in the former case. heat?' → claim at p=1.0; 'total kittification of the simcluster' → claim at p=0.999; 397 question-final posts carry the claim label; 1,710 claim-labelled posts are under 40 characters; 722 posts sit in the 0.4–0.6 probability band.
